Applying a fixed negative-binomial dipole-to-charged-particle response reproduces the rising trend of the H1 charged-particle multiplicity entropy toward smaller $x$, but does not fully describe the measured multiplicity distributions. These results demonstrate an explicit coherent encoding of finite-state dipole branching and clarify its relation to continuous-cascade fluctuations and DIS phenomenology.
item.dc:creator: Wei Kou, Xurong Chen

item.title: Interaction-Free Polarimetry
item.description: arXiv:2207.13539v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The combination of interaction-free measurement and the quantum Zeno effect has been shown to both increase the signal-to-noise ratio of imaging, and reduce the energy absorbed by the imaged object. So far, however, it has not been used for quantitative polarimetry, the reconstruction of a sample's Mueller matrix. In this paper, we extend this to the polarimetry of diattenuating samples. For polarisation components that the sample strongly absorbs, the protocol identifies the sample with far less absorbed energy than a single-pass measurement, a benefit for delicate samples probed with high-frequency radiation. For weakly absorbing components the repeated passes through the sample absorb more, so the benefit is confined to strongly diattenuating features. A Fisher-information analysis shows that, for a sample with a lossless transmitting axis, the protocol locates the absorbing axis with far fewer absorbed photons than single-pass polarimetry, while it measures partial transmittances no more efficiently per absorbed photon, and that the same sorting of lossy components to one output port responds to retardance and depolarisation.
item.dc:creator: Shushmi Chowdhury, John Rarity, Jonte R. Hance

item.title: Time Travel Paradoxes and Entangled Timelines
item.description: arXiv:2303.07635v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: For time travel to be consistent with the known laws of physics, the resulting paradoxes must be resolved. It has been suggested that the notion of parallel timelines may provide a resolution, by allowing different events to happen in different timelines. However, so far, a concrete mechanism by which parallel timelines can be created has never been satisfactorily formulated in a way that makes the relationships between the timelines clear. In this paper, we propose such a mechanism based on the Everett (many-worlds) interpretation of quantum mechanics. The timelines in our model are variants of the "worlds" of the Everett interpretation that can connect to each other via the time machine. They are created by the entanglement of the time machine with the environment and the resulting decoherence; therefore, we call them "entangled timelines" or E-CTCs. As the entanglement gradually spreads out to additional systems, the timelines spread out as well, providing a local and well-defined mechanism for branching timelines. The E-CTC model is similar to Deutsch's familiar D-CTC model but differs from it mainly by imposing a different consistency condition, based on pure states, which allows the information about the entanglement to be preserved. These differences allow us to create a clearer practical definition of the timelines and avoid some of the surprising consequences of the D-CTC model's non-linear evolution.
item.dc:creator: Barak Shoshany, Zipora Stober

item.title: Practical limitations on robustness and scalability of quantum Internet
item.description: arXiv:2308.12739v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The realization of a desirably functional quantum Internet is hindered by fundamental and practical challenges such as high loss during transmission of quantum systems, decoherence due to interaction with the environment, fragility of quantum states under measurement, etc. We study the implications of these constraints by analyzing the limitations on the scaling and robustness of the quantum Internet. Considering quantum networks, we present practical bottlenecks for secure communication, delegated computing, and resource distribution among end nodes. In particular, we show that the device-independent quantum key distribution (DI-QKD) network of isotropic states with parameter $p$ has a finite diameter depending on $p$. Motivated by the power of abstraction in graph theory (in association with quantum information theory), that allows us to consider the topology of a network of users spatially separated over long distances around the globe or separated as nodes within the small space over a processor or circuit within a same framework, we consider graph-theoretic quantifiers to assess network robustness and provide critical values of communication lines for viable communication over quantum Internet. We consider some quantum networks of practical interest, ranging from satellite-based networks connecting far-off spatial locations to currently available quantum processor architectures within computers, and analyze their robustness to perform quantum information processing tasks. Some of these tasks form primitives for delegated quantum computing, e.g., entanglement distribution and quantum teleportation, that are desirable for all scale of quantum networks, be it quantum processors or quantum Internet.
item.dc:creator: Abhishek Sadhu, Meghana Ayyala Somayajula, Karol Horodecki, Siddhartha Das

item.title: Optimized experiment design and analysis for fully randomized benchmarking
item.description: arXiv:2312.15836v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Randomized benchmarking (RB) is a widely used strategy to assess the quality of available quantum gates in a computational context. RB involves applying known random sequences of gates to an initial state and using the statistics of a final measurement step to determine an effective depolarizing error per step of the sequence, which is a metric of gate quality. Here we investigate the advantages of fully randomized benchmarking, where a new random sequence is drawn for each experimental trial. The advantages of full randomization include smaller confidence intervals on the inferred step error, the ability to use maximum likelihood analysis without heuristics, straightforward optimization of the sequence lengths, and the ability to model and measure behaviors that go beyond the typical assumption of time-independent error rates. We discuss models of time-dependent or non-Markovian errors that generalize the basic RB model of a single exponential decay of the success probability. For any of these models, we implement a concrete protocol to minimize the uncertainty of the estimated parameters given a fixed time constraint on the complete experiment, and we implement a maximum likelihood analysis. We consider several previously published experiments and determine the potential for improvements with optimized full randomization. We experimentally observe such improvements in Clifford randomized benchmarking experiments on a single trapped ion qubit at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). For an experiment with uniform lengths and intentionally repeated sequences the step error was $2.42^{+0.30}_{-0.22}\times 10^{-5}$, and for an optimized fully randomized experiment of the same total duration the step error was $2.57^{+0.07}_{-0.06}\times 10^{-5}$. We find a substantial decrease in the uncertainty of the step error as a result of optimized fully randomized benchmarking.
item.dc:creator: Alex Kwiatkowski, Laurent J. Stephenson, Hannah M. Knaack, Alejandra L. Collopy, Christina M. Bowers, Dietrich Leibfried, Daniel H. Slichter, Scott Glancy, Emanuel Knill

item.title: Quantifying the Functional Size of Large-Scale Quantum Networks
item.description: arXiv:2312.16009v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large-scale quantum networks enable distributed quantum tasks by sharing entanglement between distant nodes. Since entanglement distribution in such networks relies on stochastic local operations and classical communication (SLOCC), the resulting end-to-end entanglement degrades with path length and exhibits statistical variations, limiting the usable range while also making the quantification of its functional size challenging. Here, we develop a statistical framework to quantify a network's functional size by analyzing the statistics of end-to-end entanglement connections established through arbitrary entanglement-distribution protocols. This framework yields a global network metric in the form of the graph radius of viable regions up to which the distributed entanglement meets specified task thresholds. In addition to identifying absolute viable regions, within which a task is guaranteed to satisfy the prescribed thresholds, the framework identifies probabilistic viable regions, within which the task succeeds with a specified confidence. Further, it yields the viable node fraction, defined as the expected fraction of network nodes accessible from a given source node for the task, and reveals that network topology strongly influences the number of nodes contained within a network's viable region, even when the viable radii are identical. Applying the framework to quantum key distribution on random networks reveals sharp threshold behavior in the viable node fraction showing that small improvements in elementary-link quality can produce a rapid increase in the viable node fraction of the network. Viable regions in a quantum network obtained using our statistical framework therefore provide a task-oriented characterization of quantum-network functionality allowing comparison of entanglement-distribution strategies and network designs.
item.dc:creator: Md Sohel Mondal, Vladimir S. Malinovsky, Siddhartha Santra

item.title: Quantum squeezing amplification with a weak Kerr nonlinear oscillator
item.description: arXiv:2503.08197v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Quantum squeezed states, with biased quantum noise, have been widely utilized in quantum sensing and quantum error correction applications. However, generating and manipulating these nonclassical states with a large squeezing degree typically requires strong nonlinearity, which inevitably induces additional decoherence that diminishes the overall performance. Here, we demonstrate the generation and amplification of squeezed states in a superconducting microwave cavity with weak Kerr nonlinearity. By subtly engineering an off-resonant microwave drive, we observe cyclic dynamics of the quantum squeezing evolution in a displaced frame of the cavity. Furthermore, we deterministically realize quantum squeezing amplification by alternately displacing the Kerr oscillator using the Trotterization technique, achieving a maximum squeezing degree of 14.6 dB and a squeezing rate of 0.28 MHz. Our demonstrated displacement-enhanced squeezing operation offers a hardware-efficient approach for generating large squeezed states, promising potential applications in quantum-enhanced sensing and quantum information processing.
item.dc:creator: Yanyan Cai, Xiaowei Deng, Libo Zhang, Zhongchu Ni, Jiasheng Mai, Peihao Huang, Pan Zheng, Ling Hu, Song Liu, Yuan Xu, Dapeng Yu

item.title: Non-Perturbative Geometric Framework for Qubit Gates under Always-On Couplings
item.description: arXiv:2503.12424v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Always-on couplings in qubit arrays enable multi-qubit entanglement but also generate crosstalk. We present a geometric framework for a driven qubit at fixed detuning, in which the SU(2) evolution traces a curve on a sphere whose radius is determined by the detuning and the control pulse is the curve's geodesic curvature, reducing gate design to drawing a curve. Closed loops yield crosstalk-free single-qubit gates, with a zero-area condition for undetuned subspaces, while nonzero-area loops also permit entangling-gate constructions. The framework is non-perturbative in the conditional detuning, within a dispersive block-diagonal approximation valid when the transverse mixing $g/\Delta$ is small, and recovers perturbative dynamically corrected gate methods as its flat-space limit. Noise robustness can be imposed as an additional constraint. We show numerically that in two- and three-qubit Heisenberg chains the single-qubit gates are robust to coupling and frequency noise, and outperform a representative perturbative robust gate by over an order of magnitude where perturbation theory breaks down.
item.dc:creator: Junkai Zeng, Lin Chen, Xiu-Hao Deng

item.title: Quantitative Quantum Soundness for Bipartite Compiled Bell Games via the Sequential NPA Hierarchy
item.description: arXiv:2507.17006v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Compiling Bell games under cryptographic assumptions replaces the need for physical separation, allowing nonlocality to be probed with a single untrusted device. While Kalai et al. (STOC'23) showed that this compilation preserves quantum advantages, its quantitative quantum soundness has remained an open problem. We address this gap with two primary contributions. First, we establish the first quantitative quantum soundness bounds for all bipartite compiled Bell games via a newly formalized convergent sequential Navascu\'es-Pironio-Ac\'in (NPA) hierarchy: any polynomial-time prover's score is controlled by a finite-level hierarchy value, and finite-level convergence gives a negligible gap to the commuting quantum value, or to the tensor-product quantum value under flat optimality. Second, we develop the sequential NPA hierarchy as a computational tool of independent interest, establishing its convergence and a stopping criterion based on flatness, and identifying its conic dual as a sparse SOS hierarchy.
item.dc:creator: Igor Klep, Connor Paddock, Marc-Olivier Renou, Simon Schmidt, Lucas Tendick, Xiangling Xu, Yuming Zhao

item.title: The role of entropy production and thermodynamic uncertainty relations in the asymmetric thermalization of open quantum systems
item.description: arXiv:2510.05072v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The asymmetry between heating and cooling in open quantum systems is a hallmark of nonequilibrium dynamics. Here, we investigate the thermalization of a quantum system weakly coupled to a bosonic thermal bath under detailed balance, focusing on the entropy production rate and the quantum thermokinetic uncertainty relation (TKUR). Within the sector of states that remain diagonal in the energy basis we derive a perturbative expression for the time-dependent entropy production rate by expanding the relative entropy around equilibrium in terms of Liouvillian eigenmodes. Through this expansion, we determine that the spectral gap, the overlap of the initial state with the slowest decay mode, and the mode weight control the entropy production. Particularly for the thermal qubit, the ratio of the initial rates of heating and cooling has an exact closed form. Heating involves a higher initial entropy production, and hence faster thermalization, solely because of its larger spectral gap, i.e., the bath-temperature dependence of the dissipative rate. The TKUR is then used as a diagnostic tool that relates the asymmetry to the precision bounds on heat-current fluctuations. The analysis presented here is intended to clarify the thermodynamic origin of the asymmetry within the well-controlled Markovian case.
item.dc:creator: \'Alvaro Tejero

item.title: Learning photonic quantum states
item.description: arXiv:2510.07240v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Learning quantum state properties is both a fundamental and practical problem in quantum information theory. Classical shadows have emerged as an efficient method for estimating properties of unknown quantum states, with rigorous statistical guarantees, by performing randomized measurement on few copies of the state. With the advent of photonic technologies, formulating efficient learning algorithms for such platforms comes out as a natural problem. Here, we introduce a practical classical shadow protocol for learning photonic quantum states via randomized passive linear optical transformations and photon-number measurement. We provide rigorous theoretical guarantees showing that our scheme is sample- and time-efficient for measuring physical observables of interest. We experimentally demonstrate our photonic classical shadow protocol on both a twelve-mode and a twenty-four-mode integrated quantum processing unit, and showcase its versatility with five different applications, including Hamiltonian measurement and learning complex photonic states.
item.dc:creator: Hugo Thomas, Ulysse Chabaud, Pierre-Emmanuel Emeriau

item.title: Quantum theory of electrically levitated nanoparticle-ion systems: Motional dynamics and sympathetic cooling
item.description: arXiv:2511.21495v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop the theory describing the quantum coupled dynamics of the center-of-mass motion of a nanoparticle and an ensemble of ions co-trapped in a dual-frequency linear Paul trap. We first derive analytical expressions for the motional frequencies and classical trajectories of both nanoparticle and ions. We then derive a quantum master equation for the ion-nanoparticle system and quantify the sympathetic cooling of the nanoparticle motion enabled by its Coulomb coupling to a continuously Doppler-cooled ion. We predict that motional cooling down to sub-kelvin temperatures is achievable in state-of-the-art experiments even in the absence of motional feedback and in the presence of micromotion. We then extend our analysis to an ensemble of $N$ ions, predicting a linear increase of the cooling rate as a function of N and motional cooling of the nanoparticle down to tenths of millikelvin in current experimental platforms. Our work establishes the theoretical toolbox needed to explore the ion-assisted preparation of non-Gaussian motional states of levitated nanoparticles.
item.dc:creator: Saurabh Gupta, Bernard Faulend, Dmitry S. Bykov, Tracy E. Northup, Carlos Gonzalez-Ballestero

item.title: Blockade-induced exchange primitives for scalable neutral-atom QPU
item.description: arXiv:2511.22214v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Many quantum hardware platforms natively support either phase or exchange operations, yet converting between these two forms of control typically incurs substantial overhead. Rydberg-blockade neutral-atom arrays are highly developed for phase control. Here, controlled exchange is introduced as a native, blockade-programmed phenomenon in a collective excited manifold. Target operations are engineered such that two competing exchange pathways between |01> and |10> destructively interfere, while a single collective four-photon channel mediated by a symmetric Rydberg excitation remains resonant and drives a direct SWAP, with all other qubit configurations undergoing an identity action. Exchange conditionality follows from blockade, where exciting a control atom to a Rydberg state shifts and blocks the target collective resonance, suppressing exchange, whereas leaving the control in the ground manifold enables exchange in a single step. This approach yields a family of controlled-exchange gates with coherent average gate fidelities above 99.99% at selected operating points, while reducing circuit depth and Rydberg-state exposure time by an order of magnitude relative to decomposed implementations. Joint parameter optimization reduces sensitivity to laser-intensity fluctuations, Doppler shifts, and interatomic-distance uncertainty, with several SWAP-family gates retaining fidelities above 99.6% under realistic experimental fluctuations and Rydberg decay. Finally, the anisotropic interaction generalizes the same principle to multiplexed controlled-exchange operations, providing compact hardware-level primitives for conditional information routing in extended neutral-atom arrays.
item.dc:creator: Mohammadsadegh Khazali, Klaus M{\o}lmer

item.title: Antisymmetrization of composite fermionic states for quantum simulations of nuclear reactions in first-quantization mapping
item.description: arXiv:2512.16138v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: I present a first-quantization deterministic algorithm for antisymmetrizing a spatially separated target-projectile system containing $N_T$ and $N_p$ identical fermions, respectively. The method constructs a fully antisymmetric wavefunction from the product of two independently antisymmetrized many-body states, each of which may be a superposition of Slater determinants. The algorithm uses a Dicke-state ancilla register that coherently encodes all one-particle exchange channels between the two subsystems and, crucially, requires only single-particle swaps to generate the full antisymmetric structure. After consolidating distinct control conditions using logical or operations, the optimized circuit uses $N_TN_p$ single-particle exchanges, up to $N_p$ of which can be performed in parallel. The correct fermionic phase is incorporated through the application of $Z$ gates on $N_T$ ancillae, after which the ancilla register is efficiently uncomputed using a compact sequence of controlled operations. This construction provides a nontrivial and scalable protocol for preparing fully antisymmetric states in reaction and scattering simulations, significantly expanding the range of systems that can be addressed with first-quantized quantum algorithms.
item.dc:creator: Ionel Stetcu

item.title: Tunable many-body burst in isolated quantum systems
item.description: arXiv:2602.09665v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Thermalization in isolated quantum many-body systems can be nonmonotonic depending on an initial state. We demonstrate that a burst---a transient deviation from thermal equilibrium---can be created at a designated time from a low-entangled initial state for a nonintegrable mixed-field Ising chain, by developing a systematic numerical method to construct such a low-entangled state. Contrary to the typical spreading of information, the created burst is accompanied by a slow or even negative entanglement growth. We analytically show that a burst becomes probabilistically rare after a long time. Our results suggest that a nonequilibrium state is maintained for an appropriately chosen initial state until quantum scrambling becomes dominant. Our predictions can be tested by quench experiments with programmable quantum simulators.
item.dc:creator: Shozo Yamada, Akihiro Hokkyo, Masahito Ueda

item.title: On the emergence of quantum mechanics from stochastic processes
item.description: arXiv:2602.22095v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The stochastic--quantum correspondence reinterprets quantum dynamics in terms of an underlying stochastic process on a configuration space. We generalize its lifting prescription, overcoming restrictions on the reachable density matrices without enlarging the configuration space or its associated Hilbert space. A compatibility relation and Kraus dictionary connect stochastic kernels to completely positive, trace-preserving (CPTP) maps: every finite-dimensional kernel admits a compatible lift, and these lifts collectively encompass all quantum channels as the kernels vary. We describe sufficiently regular composable CPTP dynamics through time-local Lindblad generators. We establish that every rooted quantum dynamical family admits a stochastic realizer on the same configuration space, and that a revival of configuration-space distinguishability rules out every Markovian realizer on that space.
item.dc:creator: Jason Doukas

item.title: Quantum Riemannian Hamiltonian Descent
item.description: arXiv:2603.28624v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose Quantum Riemannian Hamiltonian Descent (QRHD), a quantum algorithm for continuous optimization on Riemannian manifolds that extends Quantum Hamiltonian Descent (QHD) by incorporating geometric structure of the parameter space via a position-dependent metric in the kinetic term. We formulate QRHD in both operator and path integral formalisms and derive the corresponding quantum equations of motion, showing that quantum corrections appear in the action integral but they are suppressed at late times by the time-dependent dissipation factor. This implies that convergence near optimal points is controlled by the classical potential while quantum effects influence early-time dynamics. By analyzing the semiclassical equation, we estimate a lower bound on the convergence time and numerically demonstrate whether QRHD works as a quantum optimization algorithm in some examples. A quantum circuit implementation based on time-dependent Hamiltonian simulation is also discussed and the query complexity is estimated.
item.dc:creator: Yoshihiko Abe, Ryo Nagai

item.title: Detection of quantum imaginarity using moments and its interferometric realization
item.description: arXiv:2604.00164v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Complex numbers, intrinsic to the formulation of quantum theory, play a pivotal role in enabling advantages across a broad range of quantum information-processing tasks. Despite their fundamental importance, practical and scalable criteria for detecting quantum imaginarity remain relatively underexplored, particularly methods that enable its identification with reduced experimental overhead. In this work, we propose a realistic and experimentally feasible method to detect quantum imaginarity using a moment-based approach. Our framework relies on experimentally accessible moments of the Kirkwood-Dirac quasiprobability distribution, enabling scalable detection in high-dimensional systems without requiring full state tomography. We then present illustrative examples to support our detection scheme. Finally, we present an interferometric scheme for measuring these moments, paving the way for experimental implementation of our detection protocol.
item.dc:creator: Sudip Chakrabarty, Saheli Mukherjee, Ananda G. Maity, Bivas Mallick

item.title: Robust quantum metrology using disordered probes
item.description: arXiv:2604.11635v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Disorder is ubiquitous in quantum devices including quantum probes designed and fabricated for quantum parameter estimation and sensing. We investigate the robustness of a quantum probe against the presence of glassy disorder. We define a disorder marker quantifying the effect of the disorder by expanding the quantum Fisher information in terms of different orders of the standardized central moments of the disorder-distributions. We classify the quantum probes in terms of the possible values of the disorder marker, and analytically show, for a disorder-sensitive probe with identical and weak disorder on all or a subset of the parameters of the probe-Hamiltonian, that the absolute value of the disorder marker exhibits a quadratic dependence on the disorder strength. We derive a robustness scale intrinsic to the probe that competes with the disorder, and provide a prescription for estimating the maximum disorder strength that the probe can withstand from the disorder-free probe-Hamiltonian for a given initial state of the probe, which can be computed without the disorder averaging. We also extend the prescription to classical Fisher information, and provide an operational perspective to the proposed marker in experiments. We demonstrate our results in the case of a single-qubit probe under disordered magnetic field, and a multi-qubit probe described by a disordered one-dimensional Kitaev model with nearest-neighbor interactions.
item.dc:creator: Vishnupriya K., Harikrishnan K. J., Amit Kumar Pal

item.title: The Quantum Kicked Rotor: A Paradigm of Quantum Chaos. Foundational aspects and new perspectives
item.description: arXiv:2604.12316v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The kicked rotor provides a simple yet powerful model for introducing many of the central concepts of classical and quantum chaos. Despite its apparent simplicity, it exhibits rich dynamical behavior and has found applications across a wide range of fields, including atomic and optical physics, condensed matter physics, and emerging quantum technologies. This chapter begins by exploring foundational ideas using the kicked rotor as a unifying framework. We first discuss the transition from regular to chaotic motion in the classical system, and then introduce key quantum phenomena such as dynamical localization and quantum resonances. Special attention is devoted to the emergence of characteristic time scales and their role in the quantum-classical correspondence. To make these ideas more concrete, we also provide a brief overview of experimental realizations of the kicked rotor and its variants, illustrating how theoretical concepts are implemented in practice. In the second part of the chapter, we guide the reader toward more recent and advanced developments. Topics include near-resonant dynamics, topological features of kicked systems, the emergence of quantum dynamical phases inferred from classical transport properties, and extensions to non-Hermitian physics. We conclude with a discussion of open problems and future perspectives, outlining directions in which the kicked rotor continues to offer valuable insights.
item.dc:creator: Giuliano Benenti, Giulio Casati, Jiangbin Gong, Zhixing Zou

item.title: Squeezing and measurement of a mechanical quadrature via PID feedback
item.description: arXiv:2604.16202v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) control is used for automatically regulating a measurable quantity to a desired setpoint. It is widely used in different types of classical control electronics. Here, we show how generalizing the feedback term in quantum systems to include derivative and integral components influences both the transient and steady-state behavior of the amplitude and squeezing of a mechanical quadrature in an optomechanical system. We show that, the derivative feedback leads to enhanced unconditional squeezing. Furthermore, we demonstrate how feedback may be employed to drive a mechanical quadrature to a desired setpoint, and to track an external force. Our findings offer new routes for an improved quantum state control and measurement precision.
item.dc:creator: Alberto Hijano, Tero T. Heikkil\"a

item.title: Quantum rotation sensing from superintegrability
item.description: arXiv:2605.09709v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Detection based on quantum principles such as entanglement has the capacity to achieve finessed levels of sensitivity, bringing transformative impacts to applications. In this study, we propose a rotation sensing protocol using an extended Bose-Hubbard model in a four-site configuration. The design, based on a simple population imbalance measurement to quantify rotation, profits from the property of superintegrability. The implementation of the sensing protocol achieves rotation-detection sensitivity scaling as $N^{-3/2}$, where $N$ is the number of particles. Remarkably, the sensitivity lies close to the quantum Cram\'er - Rao bound. Our results illustrate superintegrability opportunities for advancing the field of quantum sensing.
item.dc:creator: Leandro Hayato Ymai, Karin Wittmann Wilsmann, Joel Bacellar Neves, Arlei Prestes Tonel, Jon Links, Angela Foerster

item.title: Ancilla-Assisted Quantum Process Tomography using Bound entangled states
item.description: arXiv:2605.19182v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Lu \textit{et al.} [Ann. Phys. (Berlin) \textbf{534}, 2100550 (2022)] raised the question of whether bound entangled states can be useful for ancilla-assisted quantum process tomography (AAQPT). We answer their question in the affirmative by constructing bound entangled states that are faithful and hence allow complete reconstruction of an unknown quantum channel. We also study the effect of local filtering, which can increase the computable cross norm and realignment of a state while destroying its faithfulness. We further examine the performance of bound entangled probes, taking into account the stability of channel reconstruction rather than faithfulness alone. We find that bound entangled states can provide better-conditioned reconstruction than any separable probe, despite their entanglement being nondistillable.
item.dc:creator: Gurvir Singh

item.title: Construction of three-qubit positive-partial-transpose entangled states of rank four
item.description: arXiv:2605.19530v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multiqubit positive-partial-transpose (PPT) entangled states provide canonical examples of bound entanglement and stringent test cases for multipartite separability criteria. We study PPT entangled states of the minimum possible rank in the three-qubit system, namely rank four. In the established terminology, states with a nonzero Lorentz invariant are called type I, whereas those with a zero Lorentz invariant are called type II. Every such state constructed from an unextendible product basis (UPB) has a nonzero Lorentz invariant and hence is of type I. We give a necessary and sufficient criterion for determining whether a type-I state is SLOCC-equivalent to a PPT entangled state constructed from a UPB. For type-II states, we obtain a Bell-basis normal form and prove that it exhausts all such states up to SLOCC equivalence. We further give a necessary and sufficient condition for two states in this normal form to be SLOCC-equivalent. We also determine the range of the Lorentz invariant for multiqubit states.
item.dc:creator: Yonggang Cheng, Lin Chen

item.title: Quantum theory of a three-photon Kerr parametric oscillator: from exact solution to the Kerr-cat qutrit
item.description: arXiv:2605.21036v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We investigate the quantum properties of a nonlinear Kerr oscillator driven by a three-photon pump. We identify an exact spectral degeneracy at which the interacting ground state admits a nonperturbative analytical solution. In the large-amplitude regime, the resulting manifold becomes threefold quasi-degenerate and forms delocalized three-headed quantum superpositions. Away from the exact degeneracy, we derive an approximate description of the threefold quasi-degenerate manifold in terms of $\mathbb{Z}_3$-symmetric superpositions of squeezed coherent states. These states differ qualitatively from conventional three-component cat states due to the presence of squeezing with a distinctive parametric dependence. By varying the pump-oscillator detuning, the squeezing can be enhanced, suppressed, or even reversed, leading to a squeezing-to-anti-squeezing transition. In the large-amplitude regime, the threefold manifold defines a noise-biased bosonic qutrit, which we term a Kerr-cat qutrit. We show that photon loss predominantly induces cyclic shift errors, while clock errors are suppressed, and quantitatively characterize the resulting noise bias. We further show that the detuning controls the noise bias through the squeezing. Going beyond stabilization, we construct arbitrary operations on a single Kerr-cat qutrit together with an entangling two-qutrit gate, providing a complete set of logical operations for universal qutrit quantum computation, and validate their action through full Lindblad simulations. Our results establish the three-photon Kerr oscillator both as a rich nonlinear quantum system with analytically tractable macroscopic states and as a platform for noise-biased bosonic qutrit quantum computation.
item.dc:creator: Alessandro Bruno, Patrick P. Potts, Alexander Grimm, Matteo Brunelli

item.title: Sudden death of entanglement, rebirth of magic
item.description: arXiv:2605.22603v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Local Markovian noise cannot bring entanglement back, but it can bring magic back. Local dissipation can push a state out of the stabilizer polytope as well as in. Under independent amplitude damping, the $n$-qubit state $\alpha|0^n\rangle+\beta|1^n\rangle$ with $0<\alpha<\beta$ loses its magic for a finite interval. The coherence between its ground and fully excited configurations keeps falling throughout. Magic returns when the fully excited population falls below that coherence. The damping probabilities for entanglement death and magic rebirth obey $\gamma_e+\gamma_+=1$ for every $n\ge2$. Magic returns to the register just as its reservoirs become entangled. For a sufficiently small ground-state amplitude the register is already fully separable at rebirth. Every proper marginal is a stabilizer mixture throughout, yet a joint parity measurement followed by Clifford decoding can concentrate the reborn magic onto one qubit. With thermal relaxation and dephasing, we find a range in which magic loss is permanent for every isolated qubit, yet two qubits exposed to the same noise can regain it.
item.dc:creator: Chenfeng Cao

item.title: A framework for the evaluation of transport-induced excitations in shuttling-based ion-trap quantum processors
item.description: arXiv:2605.25118v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop a theoretical and numerical framework to analyze the effect of transport on the motional states of ions in a trapped-ion quantum processor. We decompose the shuttling protocol into primitive operations and characterize these in terms of their heating performance. Instead of having to simulate the whole transport protocol for each complete ion trajectory, the method allows us to determine the heating properties of each primitive operation separately and obtain the global result through an algebraic expression. We demonstrate our method by applying it to an 8-qubit quantum processor design based on linear transport and swap operations for all-to-all connectivity. We show how to incorporate the price of motional operations at the level of the compiler as a cost function.
item.dc:creator: Rodrigo Munoz, Phil Nuschke, Teresa Meiners, Brigitte Kaune, Christian Ospelkaus

item.title: Adaptive identification of low-degree polynomials in quantum singular value transformation: application to nonlinear quantum properties estimation
item.description: arXiv:2606.10994v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Estimating properties of unknown quantum states via quantum singular value transformation (QSVT) often requires high-degree polynomials to handle small eigenvalues of density matrices. Specifically, the existing approaches determine the polynomial degree by relying on overly conservative worst-case bounds based on the minimum non-zero eigenvalue or the rank of the density matrices. In this work, we propose a spectral cutoff method that truncates the negligible eigenvalue tail depending on the task, the target accuracy, and the state, which enables the use of significantly lower-degree polynomials. To implement this, we develop a two-stage algorithm to estimate nonlinear properties, particularly von Neumann entropy and R{\'e}nyi entropy. In the first stage, we execute a search algorithm to identify the spectral cutoff directly from the unknown quantum state. In the second stage, we estimate the nonlinear properties utilizing QSVT with the degree of the polynomial adaptively determined by the cutoff. This two-stage algorithm enables adaptive property estimation without prior knowledge of the minimum eigenvalue or the rank, using low-degree polynomials beyond conventional worst-case choices.
item.dc:creator: Jumpei Kato, Akira Tanji, Hiroyuki Harada, Kaito Wada, Kosuke Ito, Naoki Yamamoto

item.title: Locally Acting Grover Mixers for Constraint-Preserving QAOA
item.description: arXiv:2606.11530v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Grover mixer quantum alternating operator ansatz (GM-QAOA) employs the Grover mixer to confine the quantum evolution to the feasible subspace defined by the problem. Its mixing unitary, however, requires a global multi-controlled phase-shift gate acting on all qubits, resulting in substantial circuit overhead on near-term quantum devices. In this work, we propose locally acting Grover mixers with independent variational parameters, tailored to initial states that admit a product structure over disjoint qubit subsystems, which may be obtained by encoding only a subset of problem constraints into the initial state preparation. The proposed method preserves the search space defined by the initial state while reducing the mixing-circuit gate count and depth relative to the global Grover mixer, as the global multi-controlled phase-shift gate is replaced with local operations on disjoint subsystems. Numerical simulations on the exact-cover problem and the traveling salesman problem (TSP) demonstrate that the proposed method achieves solution probabilities comparable to those of the original GM-QAOA, while using shallower circuits with fewer gates. Comparisons with shared-angle local Grover and partitioned XY-ring mixers characterize the trade-offs between solution quality, circuit complexity, and optimization overhead. We further compare two constraint encoding strategies for the TSP, encoding only a subset of constraints versus all constraints into the initial state preparation, and show that the former combined with the proposed mixer can yield markedly more compact circuits at the point where comparable solution quality is achieved.
item.dc:creator: Minjin Choi, Dongkeun Lee, Junghee Ryu

item.title: Direct-Coupled Architectures for Magic-State Factories
item.description: arXiv:2606.24170v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In surface-code magic-state factories, the interface that passes level-1 T states to level 2, i.e., the transport channels, waiting spots, and $|0\rangle$ correction patches, occupies a large part of the factory area. We remove this interface by applying adaptive measurement, a principle known from gate teleportation, to the consumption of T states: in adaptive X/Y consumption, the T-state patch used for a $\pi/8$ rotation is read out in the X or Y basis depending on the merge outcome. The basis choice itself performs the $\pi/4$ correction, so no correction patch is needed and a T state can be consumed wherever it already sits. Building on this property, we present direct-coupled architectures in which level-1 suppliers are attached directly to the level-2 core. D1 consumes each T state in its supplier output slot and removes the interface entirely; D2 adds one small buffer per supplier so that the supplier continues distilling without pause. Because the method changes only how a supplied T state is consumed, it applies to the many factories that perform $\pi/8$ rotations by multi-patch Pauli measurements. As an example, we apply it to a CCZ factory and compare it with Litinski's factory under the same logical-error model and the same area accounting. For a maximum output period of 120 cycles, D1 and D2 reduce the area by 24% and 29% without increasing the space-time volume, and the smallest D1 factory is 37% smaller than the smallest Litinski design. The same approach also reduces the area of two-level T factories.
item.dc:creator: Sungyeon Kook, Yujin Kang, Ilkwon Sohn, Jun Heo

item.title: RubriQ: Rubric-Guided Group Relative Policy Optimization for Constraint-Aware Quantum Circuit Synthesis
item.description: arXiv:2607.07554v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Quantum circuits are crucial for understanding quantum algorithms and must be correct and efficient on quantum processing units (QPUs). Reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiers can train large language models (LLMs) to synthesize circuits; however, the reward system is unclear. In this study, we present RubriQ, a quantum rubric, where a verifier ensures correctness and scores assess cost. We demonstrate that, leveraging group relative policy optimization, the verifier controls correctness, while scores rank correct circuits. Our evaluation includes unitary, statevector, stabilizer-tableau, and randomized verifiers consisting of quantum Fourier transform (QFT), phase-estimation (QPE), and Trotter unitaries, along with Clifford, entanglement, unitary, arithmetic, and adder quantum circuits, up to 192 qubits. Our results show that training increases correct outputs from 7% to 91%, whereas the binary reward closes less than 10%. Notably, among verified circuits, the rubric reduces average cost by 91%. We believe our framework provides valuable insights into practical quantum computing.
item.dc:creator: Ziqing Guo, Ziwen Pan

item.title: QSTAR: Quantum Selective Transfer with Adaptive Routing
item.description: arXiv:2607.21411v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Quantum transfer learning (QTL) is commonly evaluated by replacing a classical classifier with a fixed variational quantum head, leaving unclear when quantum inference provides measurable benefit. We propose QSTAR: Quantum Selective Transfer with Adaptive Routing, which retains high-confidence classical predictions and routes low-confidence samples to a quantum fallback. Using a frozen ResNet18 backbone, we compare manually designed QTL heads, architecture-searched KetGPT heads, and parameter-matched classical baselines under consistent experimental settings. On Fashion-MNIST, standard QTL heads reach at most 59.7% accuracy and 0.564 F1-score, whereas compact KetGPT Candidate #160 reaches 80.2% accuracy and 0.800 F1-score. On the routed low-confidence subset, Candidate #160 improves accuracy over the matched MLP by 6.31, 5.38, and 3.73 percentage points at \tau=0.70, 0.80, and 0.90, respectively. At the selected operating point \tau=0.70, the adaptive system reaches 81.78% accuracy and 0.816 F1-score while routing only 36.12% of test samples to the quantum branch. Candidate #160 uses 10 quantum parameters and 9 gates, while experiments on CIFAR-10, KMNIST, and SVHN show consistent accuracy gains over the corresponding adaptive classical baselines. These results show that selective quantum invocation can reduce quantum execution while improving inference on low-confidence samples.
item.dc:creator: Saim Rehman, Nouhaila Innan, Muhammad Shafique

item.title: Improved Quantum Algorithms for Reinforcement Learning Under a Generative Model
item.description: arXiv:2608.02826v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reinforcement learning is a subfield of machine learning that studies how an agent interacts with an environment in order to extract as large a reward as possible. A standard approach to study such interaction is through Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) and the task of choosing an optimal policy---a function that tells the agent which action to take. In this work, we study two types of time-dependent MDP---finite-horizon and infinite-horizon discounted---and propose new quantum algorithms for computing approximate optimal policies. Our quantum algorithms are based on a new combination of standard value iteration and quantum subroutines like quantum mean estimation and quantum maximum finding, overall enhanced with techniques from sample-optimal classical algorithms. Our resulting query complexities improve upon previous works, thus approaching already established quantum lower bounds.
item.dc:creator: Joao F. Doriguello

item.title: Dynamical Complexity of Projected Ensembles: A Geometric Quantum State Approach
item.description: arXiv:2608.09705v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the emergence of complexity in finite-size quantum systems as their dynamics transition from closed and coherent evolution to interacting and effectively open behavior. Using a state-based geometric framework, we represent mixed quantum states as probability measures on complex projective Hilbert space. Obtained by conditioning on the environment in a fixed basis, these geometric quantum states coincide with the projected ensembles that underlie deep thermalization and emergent quantum state designs. This representation allows us to track how interactions reshape the underlying pure-state geometry. We introduce two complementary diagnostics, a distinguishability measure based on the Wasserstein distance between nearby projected ensembles, which quantifies sensitivity to initial states, and a state-space coverage index, which measures long-time exploration of the subsystem state space. Applied to the quantum kicked top, both diagnostics generally increase with interaction strength. Their dependence on environment size is structured by parity symmetry, with integer-spin systems often exhibiting greater sensitivity and state-space coverage than half-integer-spin systems. These results highlight finite-size quantum effects and provide a geometric approach to quantifying dynamical complexity deep in the quantum regime.
item.dc:creator: Komal Sah, Fabio Anza, Alexandra M. Jurgens, James P. Crutchfield

item.title: Statistical Mechanics of Non-Abelian Learnability Transitions
item.description: arXiv:2608.19325v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Monitored many-body quantum systems can undergo sharp learnability transitions characterized by how much information can be learned by the observer. When the dynamics conserves a non-Abelian charge, such as an $SU(2)$ spin, understanding how the observer learns the total charge remains an outstanding problem. Unlike the Abelian case, where charge measurements on distinct sites commute, the $SU(2)$-symmetric readouts are noncommuting fusion measurements, making learning a genuinely quantum inference problem. We propose a theory of $1+1d$ monitored quantum dynamics with $SU(2)$ symmetry, and show that it can be described by an effective replicated loop model comprised of a replica-pairing field and a diffusive ($z=2$) background sector that carries the $SU(2)$ charge and remains gapless throughout the phase diagram. Our theory predicts that the "spin-sharpening" and entanglement transitions coincide as a single transition, which is supported by numerics. Ordering of the pairing field produces volume-law entanglement and hides the background sector from measurements, leading to a learning time of $t\sim L^{3}$ for the total spin. When the pairing field disorders, the background sector alone gives logarithmic entanglement and a diffusive learning time $t\sim L^{2}$. Our analysis is controlled by a large-loop-fugacity expansion.
item.dc:creator: Ruochen Ma, Romain Vasseur

item.title: Robust Quantum Key Distribution Arbitrarily Close to Local Correlations
item.description: arXiv:2608.22603v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recently, Wooltorton et al. [Phys. Rev. Lett. 132, 210802 (2024)] and Farkas [Phys. Rev. Lett. 132, 210803 (2024)] have exhibited the mismatch between Bell inequality violations and their cryptographic application in device-independent quantum key distribution, by showing that arbitrarily close to the set of local behaviours there exist quantum correlations guaranteeing a constant rate of secret key. While these results require correlations attaining the maximum quantum value of a suitable Bell observable (aka the Tsirelson bound) and rely on a kind of ideal self-testing of a maximally entangled state and associated Bell measurement, here we show that the effect is robust: for every one of the Bell inequalities considered by Wooltorton \emph{et al.}, a constant rate of secret key ensues if the observed Bell violation is sufficiently close to the respective Tsirelson bound. For these and also the Bell inequalities of Farkas, we furthermore present numerical results based on semidefinite relaxations of the minimum min-entropy consistent with a certain Bell violation, which demonstrate that small but nonzero key rates can be guaranteed (in principle) by practical and efficient means.
item.dc:creator: Hari Krishnan SV, Andreas Winter

item.title: Electrostatic Stabilization of Near-Surface Quantum Sensors via Dielectric Interface Engineering
item.description: arXiv:2609.20137v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Control of charge-state stability in near-surface quantum defects is critical for nanoscale sensing, yet remains particularly challenging under ultra-high vacuum (UHV), where surface-induced band bending destabilizes the metrologically relevant charge-state. Here, we present a robust and reproducible approach for stabilizing shallowly implanted (< 10 nm deep) nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in near-UHV conditions (P = $3 \times 10^{-9}$ mbar) based on dielectric interface engineering. Through measurements on individually addressable NV centers, we demonstrate that a TiO2 coating on the diamond suppresses surface-induced electrostatic fields, yielding a 79% increase n NV- population and a 45% enhancement in NV-spin resonance contrast at room temperature. Coherent control measurements further reveal suppressed charge-state conversion dynamics. These results establish dielectric screening as a powerful and reproducible strategy to engineer charge transition energetics of NV centers in scanning-probe-compatible geometries under extreme conditions.
item.dc:creator: Atharva Paranjape, Kathrin K\"uster, Olga Shevstova, Lisa Ebo, Toni Hache, Klaus Kern, Rainer St\"ohr, J\"org Wrachtrup, Aparajita Singha

item.title: Simultaneous Reduction of Observables and Measured Qudits in Entanglement-Assisted Quantum Local Recovery
item.description: arXiv:2609.23316v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Let $\mathbb{F}_q$ be the finite field with $q$ elements, $q$ being a prime power. For an entanglement-assisted or unassisted stabilizer code defined by an $\mathbb{F}_q$-linear space $C\subseteq\mathbb{F}_q^{2n}$, a set of erasures and an associated repair group, we propose a procedure to compute a reduced set of observables and a reduced repair group of codeword qudits for correcting the given erasures. The computed set of observables has the smallest possible size for correcting the given erasures, within the stabilizer measurement model. The repair group is reduced by eliminating qudits that need not be measured. In classical local recovery, such symbols can be found by Gaussian elimination, although the resulting repair group need not be a smallest one. In the quantum case we eliminate an admissible set of qudits. Finding a largest admissible set is a linear matroid parity problem, and for Calderbank--Shor--Steane (CSS) codes defined by two linear codes it is a linear matroid intersection problem. Both problems are solvable in deterministic polynomial time. We give closed-form upper bounds on the size of reduced repair groups for general codes and for codes from Euclidean and Hermitian orthogonality, and, for two-code CSS codes, a sharper bound with a min--max formula. Based on these bounds, we propose quantum counterparts of the concept of dimension locality of classical local recovery.
item.dc:creator: Carlos Galindo, Fernando Hernando, Ryutaroh Matsumoto

item.title: Realizing Braided Fusion 2-Categories as (3+1)D Mixed-State Topological Orders
item.description: arXiv:2610.03864v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We construct large families of mixed-state topological orders in (3+1)D, including intrinsically mixed-state topological orders. We realize these theories by relating the data parameterizing braided fusion 2-categories to the strong higher-form symmetries and their anomalies that characterize mixed-state topological order. We focus here on bosonic theories, which include theories which admit an emergent fermion in the spectrum of line operators. Our general framework is exemplified on the lattice, where we present concrete models and identify how the data of braided fusion 2-categories are physically encoded. We then formalize this data and show that every braided fusion 2-category arises from a general construction (decoherence followed by strong and weak gauging) as the category of topological operators of a (3+1)D mixed state, with intrinsically mixed-state topological orders distinguished by the presence of strong higher-form symmetries whose anomalies cannot be realized in any (3+1)D gapped ground state. Notably, we show that (3+1)D admits a new mechanism with no (2+1)D counterpart: intrinsically mixed-state order whose topological operators braid non-degenerately, but which carries a gravitational anomaly.
item.dc:creator: Ryohei Kobayashi, Abhinav Prem, Matthew Yu

item.title: Optimal GHZ extraction from MABK violations
item.description: arXiv:2610.08516v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: For $n\geq3$ parties, we prove that the least Greenberger--Horne--Zeilinger (GHZ) extractability compatible with a Mermin--Ardehali--Belinskii--Klyshko (MABK) score between the biseparable bound and the quantum maximum equals $(1+t)/2$, where $t$ rises linearly with the score from $t=0$ to $t=1$ across this range. The minimum is over all states and binary measurements in arbitrary local dimensions, and the extractability of a state is the supremum over local channels of the overlap with the GHZ state. With a qubit at every party, the minimum is strictly larger for $0<t<1$; we determine it exactly. We construct a mixture on one qutrit and $n-1$ qubits that attains $(1+t)/2$ with measurements independent of $t$. We prove that, for $0<t<1$, its product of local ranks (ranks of its single-party reduced states), $3\cdot2^{n-1}$, is the smallest among attaining states and, for $n\geq4$, it is the only attaining state with this product, up to local isometries and party permutations. On one qutrit and $n-1$ qubits with arbitrary binary measurements, for $n\geq4$ and $t$ bounded away from zero, we prove that an extractability within a small $\varepsilon$ of $(1+t)/2$ forces trace-norm distance $O(\sqrt{\varepsilon})$ from the mixture at the same $t$, up to local unitaries, uniformly in $n$ and with optimal exponent. Since the Bell statistics do not determine the extractability, we also bound this distance for $n\geq3$ and $t>0$ by the MABK score and the expectations of five calibrated binary measurements on the qutrit, assuming known local dimensions and a known two-dimensional qutrit subspace invariant under both Bell observables of that party; the bound vanishes when these expectations equal their values in the mixture.
item.dc:creator: Avraham Kreindel (Yohananov), Aryeh Lev Zabokritskiy (Yohananov)

item.title: Sufficient quantum provenance: retained fields and certified recording precision
item.description: arXiv:2610.09931v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Quantum executions that share a provenance record can still produce different output distributions. We determine which execution details a record must retain, and at what precision, to guarantee agreement within a declared Hellinger tolerance. Under a specified channel model, a certificate combining independent stochastic mechanisms and coherent rotation differences fixes the recording precision without output simulation or explicit dependence on register dimension. For four-qubit quantum approximate optimization at depth one, a 13-bit comparison record suffices at tolerance 0.05 over a declared continuous noise range, uniformly in programmed angles for each fixed task, against 19 bits for a gate-by-gate sum over the same bin family. Pairwise separation constraints characterize sufficient field sets on finite context classes and expose omissions that pass individually but fail jointly. Separately, six-qubit measurements on an IBM Heron processor show, over six tested contexts, that raw outputs need a two-label record, supplied by qubit layout, whereas outputs after a fixed application decoder need no additional context bits, at tolerance 0.15 with 97% simultaneous confidence under stationary, independent shots. Execution records can thereby be designed to carry checkable agreement guarantees.
item.dc:creator: George Kourousias, Sergio Carrato, Roberto Pugliese, Aljo\v{s}a Hafner, Francesco Guzzi, Matteo Bill\`e, Fulvio Bill\`e, Panagiotis Dimitrakis

item.title: Secure Quantum Handshakes: Quantum Network Verification Via Simon's Algorithm
item.description: arXiv:2610.12209v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Quantum networking represents the future of secure communication, enabling fundamentally new capabilities through quantum information exchange. However, these networks require secure, high-fidelity quantum communication channels. Currently, there is no reliable method to verify whether clients entering a quantum network truly possess quantum state communication capability over robust channels. In this work, we introduce a client-validation protocol that functions as a proof-of-quantum-communication handshake. Our protocol secures a quantum network against classical spoofers, faulty quantum computers, and genuine quantum devices connecting to the network over noisy or insecure channels. We validate the efficacy of this protocol through numerical simulations under erasure, dephasing, and depolarizing noise models.
item.dc:creator: Reece Robertson, Sejal Patil, Sebastian Deffner

item.title: The Generalized BEADS Representation: A Correlation-Based Visualization of Mixed Quantum States
item.description: arXiv:2610.19054v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Quantum mechanics and particularly quantum information theory suffer from a lack of intuitive images. Visualization tools offer novel perspectives on many problems in quantum physics by revealing important properties of quantum states and processes that are otherwise obscured by abstract mathematical formalisms. Here, we extend the previously established BEADS representation of pure states to the so-called generalized BEADS representation of mixed quantum states. We introduce spherical functions, so-called beads to visualize correlation structures of mixed quantum states in an informationally complete way. A recursive optimization scheme is used to obtain minimum-entanglement pure state decompositions of all subsystems of a given N-qubit state. We show how correlation function components can be decomposed into individual contributions that correspond to different types of correlations of mixed states. This allows us to visually characterize the total correlation, genuine n-partite entanglement, nonclassical quantum-discord-type correlations as well as classical correlations. We further introduce a new quantifier for W-type entanglement for identifying W-class states. After outlining the mathematical details relevant for constructing the representation, we examine the generalized BEADS representations for various types of mixed states including product, classically correlated, separable but nonclassically correlated, as well as entangled states. As exemplary applications of the generalized BEADS representation, we showcase entanglement distillation and the effects of noise channels.
item.dc:creator: Celina Br\"autigam, Steffen J. Glaser, Dennis Huber

item.title: Recovery gates as a resource in repetition-code process tomography: exhaustive gate-optimal designs for three, five and seven qubits
item.description: arXiv:2611.08310v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Repetition-code tomography compares a code's logical channel with a reference through a decoder, almost always standard minimum-weight. We ask how many single-qubit Pauli gates it needs with the measurement basis fixed---the constraint that makes the count a resource. Exhaustive enumeration at $n=3$, $5$ and $7$, ranks decided in exact arithmetic, gives minima of $0$, $1$ and $5$ gates, against $6$, $10$ and $14$ for first-order and $6$, $50$ and $308$ for full decoding. The count depends only on how many sites are corrected, not which, so it splits into a budget and a placement that decides identifiability; more sites is not monotonically better: at $n=7$ full decoding has rank $24$ of $27$, and the $n=3$ precision curve is U-shaped under a calibration floor. The three-gate design is $9.0$ times more precise than the standard six-gate decoder at the median of $40$ working points and better at every one, by $1.8$ to $88$-fold; fixing the placement in advance gives $6.9$, or $3.1$ for a pre-commitment never worse. Two certified placements lose no direction either sees and reach $10$\,mrad within twice the shots wherever identifiable. Measuring the reference everywhere gives a $16(n+2)$-component map, full rank at $n=3$, $5$ and $7$ with no gate and $44$ to $93\%$ fewer settings, though at $n=5$ and $7$ its floor stays one and three orders above target. The optima are not covariant under chain reversal.
item.dc:creator: Long Huang

item.title: The importance of shear strain in narrow Si/SiGe quantum wells
item.description: arXiv:2611.16015v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Several heterostructure profiles have been proposed for Si/SiGe quantum wells, to improve the operation of quantum-dot spin qubits. These structures share a common goal of generating either of the two wave vectors that govern the conduction-band valley coupling, dubbed $k_0$ and $k_1$. Here, we focus on the long-wavelength $k_1$ term that couples valleys when paired with shear strain, and which governs the Dresselhaus spin-orbit coupling. We show that shear strain induced by metal top gates may be enough to activate the $k_1$ valley-coupling mechanism, mitigating the need for "ultrasharp" interfaces, as commonly assumed for large valley energy splittings. We propose a scheme featuring narrow quantum wells that does not require ultrasharp interfaces, but should still provide large deterministic valley splittings (when paired with shear strain), and large spin-orbit couplings and $g$-factor corrections, which are of great interest for experimental implementations.
item.dc:creator: Hudaiba Soomro, Talise Oh, M. A. Eriksson, Benjamin D. Woods, Mark Friesen

item.title: Gate-tunable spin splitting for Andreev spin qubits in Ge quantum well heterostructures
item.description: arXiv:2611.18888v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Ge-based super-semi heterostructures are a promising platform for implementing Andreev spin qubits (ASQs). For example, they can be isotopically purified to eliminate nuclear spins that cause decoherence. However, spin-orbit coupling (SOC), which is a key ingredient for ASQs, is cubic in momentum for hole-based materials like Ge, in contrast with more-conventional ASQ materials (e.g., InAs wires), for which the SOC is linear in momentum. In this work, we study the interplay between geometrical properties like the channel width, and gate-tunable properties like the chemical potential, on ASQ operations. Intriguingly, we find that the spin splitting in a planar Ge Josephson junction does not depend on the junction width, in contrast with InAs nanowires. We explore the possibility of exploiting this property to suppress the harmful effects of charge traps. However, this prospect is spoiled by the fact that charge traps also affect the chemical potential, in addition to the channel width. Our results provide insights into the fundamental mechanisms governing spin splitting in ASQs and offer guidance for optimizing ASQs in other materials with cubic SOC.
item.dc:creator: Avani Vivrekar, Benjamin D. Woods, Mark Friesen

item.title: Fisher-information limits of Compton polarimetry for entanglement-based positronium imaging with pixelated CZT detectors
item.description: arXiv:2611.21022v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The polarisation correlation of the two annihilation photons, measured by Compton polarimetry, has been proposed as a PET biomarker of tissue microstructure. We quantify how many events this measurement needs, what limits that number and whether a small-animal CZT system reaches tissue-level contrasts. We parameterise the measurement by the correlation coefficient $\kappa$ ($\kappa=1$ maximally entangled, $1/2$ separable), derive the classical Fisher information of double-Compton events and compare it with the quantum Fisher information, relate $\kappa$ to the annihilation channels of positronium in tissue, and simulate pixelated CdZnTe (CZT) rings. The model is validated against three published measurements and an independent GATE/Geant4 simulation. A double-Compton event carries at most 0.12-0.14 units of Fisher information about $\kappa$ and 0.015 on average, 0.1-0.6% of the quantum limit. Event-wise maximum likelihood reaches the Cramer-Rao bound, whereas the conventional ratio R needs 1.2-2.3 times as many events. The observed coefficient is $\kappa_{obs}=1-\alpha(1-\kappa_{pick})$ with a pick-off share $\alpha$ of 0.13-0.29; it is sensitive to lipid fraction but not to oxygen, and published porous-polymer data give $\kappa_{pick}$ = 0.34-0.58. In a 15-mm CZT module, ordering ambiguity, position errors and electron transport halve the information per event, and sequence reconstruction recovers it. With $^{18}$F and an eight-module ring, $\kappa$ is measured to $\pm0.01$ in a 10-mm tumour with half of its decays, whereas separating tissues by $\kappa$ alone requires 6-74 times more decays than available.
item.dc:creator: Haitao Zhou, Ruonan Wang, Jie An, Min Li, Junping Lv, Yaqiong Zhang, Hongliang Wang, Zhifang Wu, Sijin Li

item.title: Symplectic Matroids, Stabilizer Codes, and Quantum Secret-Sharing
item.description: arXiv:2611.27300v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: An $\mathbb{F}_q$-linear $[[n,k]]_q$ stabilizer code is represented by a totally isotropic subspace of $\mathbb{F}_q^{2n}$ of dimension $n-k$, whose full-rank generator matrix has nonzero maximal minors on admissible column sets forming the bases of a representable symplectic matroid. Sarvepalli asked whether graphical symplectic matroids introduced by Chow give stabilizer codes with good parameters, when a Lagrangian matroid induces a quantum access structure, which code realizes it, and which polynomial carries the weight enumerator. We answer these questions. For a $3$-connected simple graph, every representation of a graphical symplectic matroid, over any field, gives a stabilizer code of distance exactly $2$, so the girth is not a lower bound. For a represented Lagrangian matroid and a dealer, we construct the dealer-shortened stabilizer code, its logical operators, an encoding isometry and explicit recovery maps, and we show that this is the code implemented by the stabilizer state through teleportation. A set of players recovers the secret, learns nothing, or learns part of it according to a rank formula on pairs of columns, which equals its mutual information with the dealer; for graph states it becomes a cut-rank condition. Over $\F_2$ a symplectic matroid of any rank has only one representation, so the code, its access structure and its weight enumerators depend on the matroid alone; for $q\ge3$ even the enumerator does not. Circuit-induced authorized sets always reconstruct when the matroid is self-dual, but not in general, and a six-qubit graph state shows that the two access structures can differ even then. Finally, a polynomial in the ranks of column pairs determines both weight enumerators.
item.dc:creator: Sayantan Ganguly

item.title: Full-chip constrained quantum annealing via self-calibrating spin-susceptibility control
item.description: arXiv:2611.27702v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Discrete optimization in finance, power grids, and logistics requires minimizing Ising Hamiltonians under coupled linear constraints. However, quadratic-penalty formulations superimpose dense cliques that exhaust the minor-embedding capacity of sparse superconducting processors at 128-176 spins, and first-order dual subgradient schemes diverge or stall under constraint coupling. Accordingly, this study proposes a hardware-native quantum-classical closed-loop primal-dual workflow, designated as Self-Calibrating Quantum Susceptibility Quasi-Newton (SelfCal-QSQN), in which linear constraints are encoded in longitudinal fields with zero auxiliary quadratic penalty couplings and dual curvature is reconstructed from single-shot spin-fluctuation covariances. This workflow requires no slack qubits or perturbation queries. Evaluated over 891 runs on D-Wave Advantage (5,612 qubits) and Advantage2 (4,560 qubits), SelfCal-QSQN drives the pre-polish trajectory-minimum raw QPU sample violation to $0.108 \pm 0.017$ at 4,560 qubits (83.3% exact feasibility after a deterministic 1-bit polish with best-incumbent tracking, reaching 47.3% of the continuous linear-programming relaxation bound), reduces high-constraint error by 6.1- to 20.1-fold over K-scaled first-order updates, attains 5.35-fold deeper feasible energies than linear programming with the identical 1-bit polish within a 4.10-s compute-only budget at 256 spins, and achieves 95.0%-96.7% feasibility on non-native and inequality benchmarks. Moreover, the workflow is robust toward shot noise and freeze-out drift.

item.title: Tripartite entanglement dynamics following a quantum quench
item.description: arXiv:2408.12533v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We investigate the dynamics of multipartite entanglement after quenches from initial states which generate multiplets of quasiparticle excitations beyond the usual pair structure. We focus on the dynamics of tripartite entanglement through the lens of the Markov gap -- a computable quantity that signals irreducible tripartite entanglement when positive. In the tight-binding chain, we show that the Markov gap is positive at intermediate times, implying the presence of tripartite entanglement. After a time delay, the Markov gap increases and then decays at longer times, thus exhibiting an entanglement barrier. We argue that those qualitative features are consistent with an interpretation of the spreading of tripartite entanglement by triplets of tripartite-entangled quasiparticles.
item.dc:creator: Cl\'ement Berthiere

item.title: Fate of an impurity strongly interacting with a thermal Bose gas
item.description: arXiv:2508.06493v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We spectroscopically study mobile impurities immersed in a homogeneous bosonic bath (a box-trapped Bose gas), varying the bath temperature and the strength of impurity-bath interactions. We compare our results to those for a quasipure Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC), and find that for strong impurity-bath interactions, the spectra narrow with increasing temperature, while the impurity energy shift is suppressed. Near the critical temperature for condensation, many-body effects still play an important role, and only for a nondegenerate bath, the system approaches the classical Boltzmann-gas behavior. The key spectral features are reproduced within the theory of an ideal Bose polaron.
item.dc:creator: Ji\v{r}\'i Etrych, Sebastian J. Morris, Simon M. Fischer, Gevorg Martirosyan, Christopher J. Ho, Moritz Drescher, Manfred Salmhofer, Zoran Hadzibabic, Tilman Enss, Christoph Eigen

item.title: Genuine multientropy, dihedral invariants and Lifshitz theory
item.description: arXiv:2509.00593v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multi-invariants are local-unitary invariants of state replicas introduced as potential probes of multipartite entanglement and correlations in quantum many-body systems. In this paper, we investigate two multi-invariants for tripartite pure states, namely multientropy and dihedral invariant. We compute the (genuine) multientropy for Lifshitz groundstates, and obtain its analytical continuation to noninteger values of R\'enyi index. We show that the genuine multientropy can be expressed in terms of mutual information and logarithmic negativity, a relation that also holds for stabilizer states. For general tripartite pure states, we demonstrate that dihedral invariants are related to R\'enyi reflected entropies. In particular, we show that the dihedral permutations of replicas are equivalent to the reflected construction, or alternatively to the realignment of density matrices.
item.dc:creator: Cl\'ement Berthi\`ere, Paul Gaudin

item.title: Predicted high-$T_{\rm c}$ superconductivity above 130 K in metastable cubic MH$_4$ compounds at ambient pressure
item.description: arXiv:2511.04222v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Hydrides have long been considered promising candidates for achieving room-temperature superconductivity; however, the extremely high pressures typically required for high critical temperatures remain a major challenge in experiment. Here, we use high-throughput first-principles calculations to propose a class of high-$T_{\rm c}$ ambient-pressure superconductors with MH4 stoichiometry. These hydrogen-based compounds adopt the bcc PtHg4 structure type, in which hydrogen atoms occupy the one-quarter body-diagonal sites of metal lattices, with the metal atoms acting as chemical templates for hydrogen assembly. Through comprehensive first-principles calculations, we identify three promising superconductors, PtH4, AuH4 and PdH4, with superconducting critical temperatures of 84 K, 89 K, and 133 K, respectively, all surpassing the liquid-nitrogen temperature threshold of 77 K. The remarkable superconducting properties originate from strong electron-phonon coupling associated with hydrogen vibrations, which in turn arise from phonon softening in the mid-frequency range. Moreover, ab initio molecular dynamics simulations demonstrate that PtH4 remains kinetic stable at 300 K over 20 ps, with no atomic diffusion observed.
item.dc:creator: Xinxin Li, Weishuo Xu, Zengguang Zhou, Jingming Shi, Hanyu Liu, Yue-Wen Fang, Wenwen Cui, Yinwei Li, Miguel A. L. Marques

item.title: A van der Waals photon-ratchet for enhancing spin defect emission and quantum sensing
item.description: arXiv:2602.02256v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Spin defects in two-dimensional materials are promising platforms for quantum information technologies and nanoscale sensing. The negatively charged boron vacancy (VB-) in hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) is particularly attractive due to its sensitivity to temperature, magnetic fields, and pressure, but its application is limited by intrinsically weak photoluminescence (PL). Here we demonstrate a van der Waals heterostructure that enhances the PL intensity of VB- by up to 45x at 4 Kelvin while preserving compatibility with ultrathin optoelectronic platforms. A type-I band alignment at the PbI2-hBN interface facilitates efficient interlayer coupling to the defect, and strong spectral overlap supports fluorescence resonance energy transfer. Ab initio calculations indicate that this coupling enables a photon-ratcheting mechanism, in which optical absorption in PbI2 generates a nonlinear polarization that drives VB- excitation. This process is consistent with interlayer energy transfer while maintaining minimal electronic and spin hybridization and preserving optically detected magnetic resonance (ODMR) contrast. The heterostructure further exhibits improved sensitivity to external magnetic fields. These results establish a route for the enhancement of defect emission via interlayer optical coupling and introduce a general materials strategy for amplifying weak quantum defect signals in nanomaterials.
